transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Members of Congress are preparing to question Jensen Wong next week behind closed doors
as the incoming Democratic majority condemns his reinstatement as NVIDIA CEO and President
Trump's endorsement of Wong.
At a news conference today, Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked about the Justice Department's
response to reports that Wong had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and could pose
a national security risk.
To the extent that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes
or something like this, that's something that I would have certainly told the President
had it been true.
So had Wong been investigated?
Excuse me?
Had Wong been investigated?
I'm not going to talk about investigation, but what does that mean, had Wong been investigated?
For what?
Yesterday, President Trump said there was no government evidence, Wong had done anything
unlawful.
He told CNBC he worked to convince NVIDIA's board to reinstate Wong, whom the President
has consulted on AI and tech policies.
A jury in New York found the Chinese firm Huawei Technologies guilty of conspiracy to
steal trade secrets and bank fraud.
But the major equipment provider for wireless telecom networks has been cleared of the most
serious charge of criminal racketeering conspiracy to steal intellectual property from U.S. companies.
In a statement, Huawei says charges are without legal or factual merit.
King Tides, the biggest tides of the year, pose major flood risks on both U.S. coasts
this week.
They could break decades-old records in Northern California over the Thanksgiving holiday.
The San Francisco Bay Area's tides could peak tomorrow at 2.8 feet above normal.
Evacuations are underway in Humboldt County, near the Oregon border.
Washington state ferries canceled several sailings.
U.S. officials are trying to calm public health fears over controlled detonation tomorrow morning
in Iowa.
And Pierre's Quill Lawrence reports the Army held a public briefing about the plan to destroy
an explosive stockpile in Middletown.
The possible toxic fallout from detonating a stockpile of unstable explosives has raised
concerns for people and livestock, some of whom have been advised to evacuate.
At the briefing, Army Major General Eric Shirley said the ordnance could explode spontaneously
if it's not destroyed now.
"We know and are confident and have the full concurrence of all the agencies who have
been participating in this, that the controlled detonation is absolutely the only way to go."
This comes after days of confusion and President Trump saying he would blame the incoming Democratic
Governor-elect of Iowa for any harm if the explosion were delayed.
The Army has been aware of the danger since March and later discarded a plan to use chemicals
to neutralize the stockpile.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
U.S. stocks end the day mixed with the NASDAQ closing down 356 points, or 1.5 percent.
The Dow closed up 424 points.
This is NPR News.
There are signs the next presidential campaign is getting underway.
There's NPR's Tamara Keith.
Democratic and Republican politicians are promoting new books and sharing thoughts about
lessons from the midterms while playing coy about their presidential ambitions.
In no time, those pretenses will be dropped as campaigns begin in earnest.
The Democratic National Committee has announced its 2028 presidential debate schedule, a dozen
debates with as many as 20 candidates allowed to qualify.
The first one is set for next June.
The Republican Party debate schedule won't be announced until early next year after a
contested election for chair of the Republican National Committee.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
This year's bobcat season in Indiana is cut short.
After licensed hunters and trappers exceeded the state's quota, more than 400 bobcats have
been killed.
Here's WFIU's Ethan San Weiss.
"Once nearly hunted to extinction in the state, bobcat numbers are now stable," says
Jerryann Albers, fur bearer and game bird program leader at the Indiana Department of
Natural Resources.
"They're a great success story and they've recovered well and obviously we are going
to keep that in mind.
The people of Indiana value bobcats and we don't want them to go extinct again."
It's the second hunt since bobcats were removed from the endangered species list in Indiana
in 2005.
This season's quota was 150 higher than last year, more than the department thinks the
population can sustain in the long term.
But it says it will adjust next year's limit based on a post-season survey.
For NPR News, I'm Ethan San Weiss in Bloomington, Indiana.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.
Unregulated merchant cash advances are trapping small businesses in crushing debt.
One business owner learned the hard way.
"This plan only works on naive and honest people."
On the Sunday story, inside the unregulated world of merchant cash advances, the Sunday
story from the Up First podcast, listen now on the NPR app.

topics.text: Congress to question NVIDIA CEO Jensen Wong behind closed doors next week after reinstatement
Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Justice Department response to reports on Wong and Chinese spy
Jury finds Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, cleared of racketeering
King Tides bring record flood risks to Northern California and Pacific Northwest coasts this week
Army plans controlled detonation of explosive stockpile in Middletown, Iowa, amid public health concerns
U.S. stocks end mixed, NASDAQ down 1.5 percent while Dow closes up 424 points
Democratic National Committee announces 2028 presidential debate schedule, first debate next June
Indiana bobcat hunting season cut short after hunters exceed state quota of 400-plus kills
Unregulated merchant cash advances trap small businesses in crushing debt, per NPR Up First story
